title: Smoked Lamb Chops with Mint Chimichurri
summary: The fast luxury cut. Frenched rib chops kissed with smoke, seared hot, finished with a bright mint chimichurri.
story: Fancy enough for company, easy enough for a weeknight. The smoke stays light, the sear makes the crust, and the chimichurri cuts right through the richness.

items: 8 frenched lamb rib chops, about 1 1/2 inches thick

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Season the chops with olive oil, salt, pepper, granulated garlic, and rosemary. Rest at room temp 30 minutes while the pit heats.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 225°F until the chops read 120°F inside, about 30 to 40 minutes.

steps.title: Sear
steps.body: Screaming hot — 60 to 90 seconds per side — until the crust darkens and the center reads 130-135°F.

steps.title: Chimichurri
steps.body: While the chops smoke, blitz the chimichurri ingredients until just combined — you want texture, not baby food.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rest the chops 5 to 10 minutes, then spoon the chimichurri over and serve.

proTips.text: Chops cook fast — the thermometer matters more here than anywhere. They go from perfect to overdone in minutes.
Frenched bones make a great handle. Let people eat with their hands.
Make extra chimichurri. It goes on everything for the next three days.

title: Smoked Stuffed Thanksgiving Turkey
summary: The centerpiece. Dry-brined overnight, stuffed and smoked low, finished hot for crisp skin — with dressing in a pan alongside catching the drippings and the smoke.
story: This is the turkey people talk about all year. The bird gets the cavity stuffing, the rest of the dressing goes in a pan on the smoker — best of both worlds — and a hot finish crisps the skin.

items: 1 lb cornbread, crumbled and dried overnight
1 lb white bread cubes, dried overnight
2 Tbsp fresh sage, chopped (or 2 tsp dried)
3 to 4 cups warm turkey or chicken broth

steps.title: Dry brine
steps.body: Mix the salt, brown sugar, pepper, poultry seasoning, and granulated garlic. Rub all over the bird, inside and out. Refrigerate uncovered 12 to 24 hours.

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Rinse off the brine and pat dry. Rub the softened butter under the breast skin and the olive oil all over the outside.

steps.title: Inject
steps.body: Stir the Creole seasoning and chicken broth into the melted butter. Inject the breast in a grid pattern, about every 2 inches — the breast is the part that dries out first.

steps.title: Stuff loosely
steps.body: Fill the cavity about two-thirds full with dressing — packed stuffing won't cook through. Truss the legs.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 275-300°F with apple or cherry until the breast reads 150°F, about 3 1/2 to 4 1/2 hours.

steps.title: Crisp the skin
steps.body: Run the pit up to 375-400°F (or move the bird to a 400°F oven) for the last 30 to 45 minutes, until the skin tightens and browns and the breast hits 165°F — and the stuffing in the cavity reads 165°F.

steps.title: Pan dressing
steps.body: Put the rest of the dressing in a buttered foil pan and smoke it alongside the bird for the last 90 minutes, stirring once.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 30 to 45 minutes tented in foil before carving.

proTips.text: The stuffing inside the bird MUST hit 165°F — that's the food-safety line. Thermometer in the center of the cavity stuffing.
The Creole butter injection is non-negotiable on the breast. It's the leanest part of the bird and the first thing to dry out.
The hot finish is what saves the skin. Low smoke alone leaves it rubbery — that last blast at 375-400°F tightens and browns it.
Don't overstuff. A loosely filled cavity cooks through; a packed one stays raw in the middle while the breast dries out.
Save the carcass. Smoked turkey stock is liquid gold for gumbo.

title: Fresh Cranberry-Orange Relish
summary: The bright counterpoint to a rich smoked turkey. Raw cranberries and a whole orange pulsed with sugar — tart, sweet, and bitter in all the right places.
story: Make it the day before; it gets better overnight. The orange peel is the secret — don't peel it.

items: 1 bag (12 oz) fresh cranberries, rinsed and picked over
1 whole navel orange, quartered (peel and all — seeds removed)

steps.title: Pulse
steps.body: Pulse the cranberries and orange quarters in a food processor until finely chopped — not pureed. You want texture.

steps.title: Sweeten
steps.body: Stir in the sugar and the pinch of salt. Start with 3/4 cup; taste and add more if you like it sweeter.

steps.title: Fold
steps.body: Fold in the pecans if using.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Refrigerate overnight. The flavors marry and the sugar pulls the juices out.

proTips.text: The orange peel is the secret — don't peel it. That's where the bitter-orange perfume lives.
This freezes beautifully. Make a double batch and freeze half for Christmas.
Leftover relish on a turkey sandwich with mayo is a top-five sandwich experience.

title: Smoked Oyster Casserole
summary: The sleeper hit of the holiday table. Smoky oysters layered with buttery crackers and cream, finished on the smoker until bubbly and golden.
story: The people who wrinkle their nose at oysters always come back for seconds.

items: 2 cans (8 oz each) smoked oysters, drained (or 1 pint fresh oysters, smoked 30 minutes first)
2 sleeves butter crackers (like Ritz), crushed coarse

steps.title: Butter the dish
steps.body: Butter a cast iron skillet or baking dish.

steps.title: Layer
steps.body: Layer half the crushed crackers on the bottom. Scatter the oysters over, drizzle with half the melted butter.

steps.title: Pour
steps.body: Pour the cream and Worcestershire evenly over the top. A few shakes of hot sauce.

steps.title: Top
steps.body: Top with the remaining crackers and the rest of the melted butter.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 300°F until bubbly and golden on top, 30 to 40 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes, serve with lemon wedges.

proTips.text: Don't oversmoke it — the oysters are already smoked. You're just warming everything through and marrying the flavors.
Butter crackers beat saltines here. The richness is the whole point.
This reheats great. Make it in the morning, warm it back up when the turkey rests.

milestones.label: Layered
milestones.hint: Crackers, oysters, cream in the skillet.

title: Smoked Chicken Wings
wood: Cherry for color, hickory for punch
summary: The cook every pit needs. Smoke first for flavor, finish hot for skin that actually snaps — then toss in whatever sauce the crowd wants.
story: Pat them dry, hit them with baking powder and rub, and don't you dare sauce them before the crisp.

items: 4 lbs chicken wings, split into flats and drumettes, tips removed
2 Tbsp Ember House Rub (or SPG, or lemon-pepper poultry rub)
Your favorite wing sauce, warmed (Buffalo, BBQ, garlic-parmesan — your call)
Ranch or blue cheese, for serving

steps.title: Dry
steps.body: Pat the wings very dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.

steps.title: Season and rest
steps.body: Toss with the baking powder and rub until evenly coated. Rest uncovered in the fridge 2 to 4 hours (overnight is even better).

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 275°F until the wings read 165°F, about 1 1/2 to 2 hours.

steps.title: Crisp
steps.body: Crank the pit to 400°F+ for 10 to 15 minutes, until the skin tightens and crackles.

steps.title: Sauce
steps.body: Toss in warm sauce — or serve dry with sauce on the side. Ranch and celery alongside.

proTips.text: The baking powder is the cheat code. It raises the skin's pH so it browns and crisps instead of going rubbery.
Never sauce before the crisp. Sauce after, always — wet skin never crisps.
These reheat in an air fryer better than fresh out of most ovens. Make extra.

title: Smoked Queso
summary: The dip that disappears first at every cookout. Velveeta, pepper jack, smoked Gouda, sausage, and Rotel, smoked in a foil pan until it's one bubbling golden pot.
story: Scoop with tortilla chips. Stir it while it smokes and don't skip the Velveeta.

items: 1 lb ground breakfast sausage, browned and drained
2 cans (10 oz each) Rotel tomatoes with green chiles, undrained
1 can (4 oz) diced jalapeños, drained (optional, for heat)

steps.title: Brown the sausage
steps.body: Brown the sausage in a skillet, breaking it up fine. Drain well.

steps.title: Load the pan
steps.body: Dump everything into a large disposable foil pan: Velveeta, pepper jack, smoked Gouda, sausage, Rotel, jalapeños if using, and the milk.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250°F, stirring every 20 to 30 minutes, until fully melted and bubbly — about 90 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve straight out of the pan with tortilla chips.

proTips.text: Don't skip the stirring. The edges melt first and the middle needs help catching up.
Velveeta is non-negotiable here. Real cheese alone breaks and goes greasy — the Velveeta keeps it smooth.
Add more jalapeño if you want it, or swap in habanero if you're feeling brave. Whichever you choose, dice it fine and stir it in with the rest.
Leftovers (if you're lucky) reheat with a splash of milk, stirred over low heat.

title: Smoked Bologna
summary: Oklahoma prime rib. A whole bologna chub scored in diamonds, rubbed down, and smoked until the outside goes dark and crusty and the inside stays juicy. Slice it thick for sandwiches — this is the one that makes people laugh until they taste it.
story: Serve on white bread with yellow mustard. Don't knock it till you've had it off the pit.

items: 1 whole all-beef bologna chub, 4–5 lbs (not sliced)
1/4 cup yellow mustard, as a binder
1/4 cup Ember House Rub (or your favorite pork rub)
White bread and yellow mustard, for serving

steps.title: Score the chub
steps.body: Peel the casing off the bologna chub if it has one. Score the outside in a diamond pattern, about 1/4 inch deep — this is where the bark builds and the smoke gets in.

steps.title: Bind and rub
steps.body: Slather the whole chub with yellow mustard, then coat it heavy with the rub. Get it in the scores.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F until the outside is dark mahogany with a solid bark — about 3 to 4 hours. It won't take much more color after hour three, so don't chase it.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes, then slice 1/2-inch thick. Serve on white bread with mustard.

proTips.text: All-beef is the move. The cheap mixed-meat chubs shrink up and split on the pit.
The bark is the whole point — wrapping steams it soft.
Yes, it's bologna. No, nobody's laughing after the first bite.
Leftover slices are gold in a hot skillet the next morning, crisped up for breakfast sandwiches.

milestones.label: Scored and rubbed
milestones.hint: Diamonds cut, mustard and rub on.

title: Smoked Trout
summary: Delicate, smoky, and dead simple. A quick brine, a light smoke, and you've got trout that flakes apart and eats just as good cold the next day on crackers. The hardest part is not eating it all standing at the pit.
story: Serve warm with lemon, or chill it and eat it cold on crackers.

items: 4 whole trout, cleaned (about 12 oz each), or 8 fillets

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Stir the water, salt, brown sugar, and pepper until dissolved. Submerge the trout and brine in the fridge for 2 hours — no longer, or it goes too salty.

steps.title: Dry and form the pellicle
steps.body: Rinse the fish quick under cold water and pat dry. Lay on a rack in the fridge uncovered for 1 hour so the surface gets tacky. That's the pellicle — smoke sticks to it.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 200°F until the thickest part hits 145°F — about 2 to 3 hours depending on size. The flesh should flake easy.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve warm with lemon, or chill it and eat cold on crackers.

proTips.text: The pellicle step matters. Wet fish takes smoke unevenly and the skin goes rubbery — tacky skin takes smoke like a champ.
Don't oversmoke it. Trout is delicate; heavy smoke bulldozes the flavor. Light wood, light hand.
The 2-hour brine is a ceiling, not a floor. Small fillets can go 90 minutes.
Leftover smoked trout mashed with cream cheese, lemon, and dill makes a spread that'll ruin store-bought dip for you.

title: Brown Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies with Pecans
finish: Deep golden crisp edges, chewy centers
summary: Nutty brown butter, melty chocolate, toasted pecans, and a hit of flaky salt — with crisp edges and a chewy middle. These are the cookies that make people ask for the recipe before they finish chewing.
story: The extra yolk and the pan rest are what get you the chew. Pull them when the centers look just barely soft.

items: 2 large eggs plus 1 yolk, room temperature
1 1/2 cups semisweet chocolate chips or chunks
1 cup pecans, toasted and roughly chopped

steps.title: Brown the butter
steps.body: Melt the butter in a light-colored saucepan over medium heat, swirling, until it foams, then turns amber with brown specks and smells nutty — about 5–7 minutes. Pour into a bowl and cool 15 minutes.

steps.title: Mix the dough
steps.body: Whisk the brown butter with both sugars until smooth. Beat in the eggs, yolk, and vanilla. Stir in the flour, baking soda, and kosher salt just until no dry streaks remain. Fold in the chocolate and pecans.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest the dough 30 minutes at room temp — the flour hydrates and the flavor deepens.

steps.title: Scoop and bake
steps.body: Scoop 2-tablespoon balls onto parchment-lined sheets, 2 inches apart, and press each one down slightly with your palm — flatter cookies crisp at the edges. Sprinkle with flaky salt. Bake at 350°F for 12–14 minutes, until the edges are deep golden and crisp but the centers still look just barely soft.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool on the pan 10 minutes (they crisp up as they cool), then move to a rack.

proTips.text: Don't walk away from the butter. It goes from brown to burnt fast — pull it when it smells like hazelnuts.
The 30-minute rest is the difference between a good cookie and the one people talk about.
Toast the pecans in a dry skillet 3–4 minutes until fragrant. Raw pecans taste like nothing next to brown butter.
Crisp-chewy is a cooling trick as much as a baking one: pull them when the centers look just barely soft, and the 10-minute pan rest sets the crisp edge while the middle stays chewy.

title: Banana Split Cake
summary: The icebox classic: buttery graham crust, a tangy cream-cheese filling, bananas, pineapple, Cool Whip, and cherries on top. No oven, no fuss — just chill and slice.
story: The cream cheese layer is the whole thing — don't skimp it and don't swap it for pudding mix.

items: 2 packages (8 oz each) cream cheese, softened
1 can (20 oz) crushed pineapple, drained well

steps.title: Make the crust
steps.body: Mix the crumbs, melted butter, and sugar; press firmly into a 9x13 pan. Chill 15 minutes.

steps.title: Make the filling
steps.body: Beat the cream cheese, softened butter, powdered sugar, and vanilla until completely smooth. Spread over the chilled crust.

steps.title: Layer the fruit
steps.body: Layer the banana slices over the filling, then spread the drained pineapple over the bananas.

steps.title: Top and chill
steps.body: Spread the Cool Whip over the top, edge to edge. Chill at least 4 hours — overnight is better.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Top with cherries, nuts if using, and a drizzle of chocolate syrup. Slice and serve cold.

proTips.text: Drain that pineapple like you mean it — squeeze it in a clean towel. Wet pineapple makes a soggy cake.
Toss the banana slices in a little lemon juice if you're making it ahead; keeps them from browning.
The cream cheese layer is the whole thing. Don't skimp it and don't swap it for pudding mix.
Chill it overnight. It slices clean and the flavors settle together.

title: Peach Baked Beans
summary: Sweet peaches meet smoky bacon and brown sugar in beans that go from side dish to the thing people ask about. Built for the smoker, but the oven works fine.
story: Bush's Brown Sugar beans and peach pie filling do the heavy lifting — the pit does the rest.

items: 2 cans (28 oz each) Bush's Brown Sugar baked beans
1 can (21 oz) peach pie filling, roughly chopped
Salt and black pepper to taste

steps.title: Crisp the bacon
steps.body: Cook the chopped bacon until crisp. Pull it out and leave the drippings in the pan.

steps.title: Soften the onion
steps.body: Sauté the onion (and bell pepper, if using) in the drippings until soft, about 5 minutes.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Stir everything into a 9x13 pan or cast-iron skillet: beans, pie filling, brown sugar, BBQ sauce, mustard, molasses, paprika, bacon, and onion. Season with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Bake or smoke
steps.body: Bake at 350°F for about 1 hour, until thick and bubbly with a caramelized top — or smoke at 275°F for 2 hours for extra pit flavor.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes. They thicken as they cool.

proTips.text: The Bush's beans and pie filling already bring sweetness, so the added brown sugar is cut back — taste before you add more.
Chop the pie filling a little; the peach slices are big and spread better cut down.
These are better the next day. Make them ahead and reheat.
If they get too thick, splash in a little water or peach juice.

title: Key Lime Coleslaw
summary: Bright, tangy, and cool — key lime juice and zest cut through rich smoked meat like nothing else. Built for pulled pork sandwiches and fish tacos.
story: Bottled key lime juice is fine — nobody's squeezing 30 key limes on a weeknight.

items: 1 bag (14 oz) coleslaw mix (or 1 small head cabbage, shredded, plus 1 grated carrot)
1/4 cup key lime juice (about 6–8 key limes)

steps.title: Make the dressing
steps.body: Whisk the mayo, sour cream, key lime juice, zest, sugar, salt, and pepper until smooth.

steps.title: Toss
steps.body: Toss with the slaw mix, grated bell pepper, green onions, and cilantro until everything's coated.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Chill at least 1 hour — it gets better as it sits.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Toss again before serving. Taste and add more lime or salt.

proTips.text: Bottled key lime juice is fine — nobody's squeezing 30 key limes on a weeknight.
Don't dress it more than 4 hours ahead or it goes watery. An hour is the sweet spot.
This is the slaw for pulled pork sandwiches and blackened fish tacos.
